utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the witness brought in, please. (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the interpreters and to the court stenographers. I want to be sure that everyone can hear me. Good afternoon to the Prosecution counsel, to Defence counsel, and good afternoon to our witness, whose redirect examination by the Defence should be completed today. Mr. Nobilo said that he would finish in about one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you agree, after a break, we will see whether the Judges are going to ask any questions today or whether they aren't, and if you agree, after a break, we can have a Status Conference in closed session because we're beginning a new sequence in this trial, that is, the last straight line. I think that you can proceed, Mr. Nobilo, if the witness is ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Last time, we handed in a new document, but we didn't manage to have it distributed, so I would like to ask the registrar to have it organised now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Defence Exhibit 578, 578A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is document 578, and this is a copy of the 419th page of General Bobetko's book. This is combat action that we are talking about, but would you please focus your attention on the organisation of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. This provides information about the organisation of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. Please tell the Court, the administration of SIS and the administration of the military police, where are they in this structure, that is my first question, that is to say, within the general staff or outside of the general staff, and, secondly, was the HVO organised along these lines, that is to say, in accordance with the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You might separate the questions. If the Prosecution had asked questions that long, you would have gotten up immediately and said that the accused was being asked too many questions at the same time. So try to start with the first question and then move to the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I took into account the fact that the witness is well-trained by now. He knew how to take five questions at a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, I think we can ask the General to tell the Court the following: SIS and the administration of the military police, where are they, from the point of view of the organisation of the Ministry of Defence in accordance with this document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, in accordance with this document, the military police administration and the SIS administration is in the organisational structure of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and they are outside the organisational structure of the main staff of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where is the administration of the military police and where is the SIS administration? Which numbers are these?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They are in the organisational structure of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia under number 3 and number 7 respectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Question number two: If we look at this model where SIS and the military police administration are outside the main staff, this model applied by the Croatian army, was that a model for the HVO as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the situation was identical in the HVO. In terms of organisation, it was set up in accordance with the organisation of the Croatian army, so that is to say that in the HVO as well, the administration for security and the administration for military police were outside the organisational structure of the main staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to have a new document distributed, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Defence Exhibit 579.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, first of all, I wish to ask you the following: This organisational pattern of your main staff, I mean, I did this in accordance with your instructions; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court what this document represents?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the organisational structure of the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, and it represents my assistants. We see here the security assistant, then the logistics assistant, Franjo Sliskovic, and then the health assistant, the chief of headquarters, then the assistant for personnel affairs, and the assistant for information and propaganda activity. Within the composition of the headquarters, there is the following structure: The assistant for general affairs, the assistant for the operations and education section, then the department for military branches, and the military intelligence department, and they are within the staff that is headed by Franjo Nakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the point of view of hierarchy, who followed you from the point of hierarchy, line number 1, line number 2, or line number 3?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The chief of staff of headquarters is the first one after me, that is to say, he is my next in command, and he was also my deputy, and then there was my immediate team consisting of assistants, but the security assistant was directly subordinated to the chief of the security service. The next level are the heads of departments who are subordinated to the chief of headquarters, the chief of staff, not to me directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who made up the team of the commander, and they made an effort to meet every morning, if possible?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those are the assistants, that is to say, Ante Sliskovic, Franjo Sliskovic, Dr. Drago Dzambas, Franjo Nakic, Zoran Pilicic, and Marko Prskalo. That is this structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period from the 16th to the 19th of April, 1993, why was Slavko Marin practically your next in command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ex officio, when the chief of headquarters is absent, then he is replaced by Slavko Marin, and then from the 16th to the 19th of April, Franjo Nakic was blocked in his family home by the BH army because of the conflict that was going on, so he could not reach Vitez. He could not reach the headquarters at the Vitez Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like a new document to be handed out, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have a question, General Blaskic. Mr. Sliskovic was in your office every day or every morning. If you were to ask him questions about this or that crime, or this or that investigation, would he sometimes answer by saying, "I'm not going to answer because I am directly subordinate to Mostar"? Because he was in your office every morning. Mr. Sliskovic, according to the interpretation I received, he would come to your office every morning. Did he work with you? Was he there in complete silence, saying "I'm not interested in the hierarchy and that's not something I get involved in"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, priority was always given to his chain of command from Mostar, and he was the assistant for security in my command, and if I would send in a request and if that request was not in contrast to the instructions he had received from Mostar, then he would not tell me that the Mostar office had priority. But there were such cases when he would say, "I got instructions that are not like that, and I'm duty-bound to act on those instructions, that is to say, the instructions I got from the office in Mostar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But then you're confirming that in the crucial period, when you seem to have asked for an investigation on Ahmici, an oral request, he was there every morning?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He came to headquarters, he carried out his duties, he informed me, and, finally, he also informed me about the problems we had in relation to the investigation materials, that he had received orders to send the investigation materials to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But when you would give out the verbal orders, from the very start, would he say, "Well, Tihomir Blaskic, don't be concerned with that because that is the responsibility of Mostar, and that's how things are," because he would come to you every morning, that's what struck me in your answer, he would come to your meeting every morning. He had to be there for some reason.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From that first order I had issued, for example, he was practically at every meeting every morning, and he did not present that kind of a report, saying, "You are not supposed to do anything. I'm going to look into this with Mostar." So not at that point, moment. Truth to tell, after a longer period of time, he did submit a first report about the investigation. This was the end of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Here's my final question: Am I wrong when I say that when you would speak to him about Ahmici, he would have to answer you, but that sometimes he might not answer you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At any rate, Mr. President, the security service had priority; that is to say, that if he would receive orders from the security service, that he should not give me an answer, he would tell me quite openly, "I received orders from my superiors and I cannot tell you about this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which therefore means that -- that's what I wanted to know. He never said that "I don't want to answer you because Mostar forbade me from doing so," that he was able to answer you; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that is what he actually told me, that he could not, for example, give me a file, that he had sent it to his superiors in Mostar, and whenever he would receive instructions from Mostar that were contrary to my orders, he would inform me about this, and I would remain without an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General, I have another question I would like to ask you. Ante Sliskovic was the individual who said to you that he could not give you the results of the investigation into Ahmici because he had sent that information to Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because he had sent the entire file to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: There is a proverb which says that anything can happen a first time. The second time, anyone who wants to fall falls. Why did you ask for the investigation into Stupni Do, ask that same person about the investigation into Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall having asked the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: If I remember correctly -- perhaps I'm wrong -- but I think I remember that you asked for the investigation into what happened in Stupni Do of your assistant for security, and the result was the same; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not testify about that, Your Honour. I did not carry out an investigation on Stupni Do. As far as I remember, it was carried out by the security service together with its officials because, as far as Stupni Do is concerned, when it happened, I thought that this was a military action between the BH army and the HVO, and the source of this information was from the main staff because I was not in direct communication with Kiseljak so that I could check it out myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So that from your perspective, you did not ask for an investigation into what had happened at Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, I was cut off in Vitez and an investigation about these events was carried out by the relocated headquarters of the main staff in Kiseljak. I do not know who was there and who was in charge of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I could ask the question in a different way: Could one say that on other occasions you asked for investigations, investigations of other events, a request that you made of Ante Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As regards all major events, I tried to have Ante Sliskovic carry out an investigation, although it is the civilian and the military police that most often started investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But I have in my mind something else. Let me look at my notes. But I think -- I am remembering about an attack on another village for which an investigation was asked of Ante Sliskovic. I am asking you whether, beyond Ahmici, you asked for other investigations to be carried out and that you asked your assistant for security to do that.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I asked for other investigations to be carried out. This had to do with the attack on Stari Vitez towards the end of July, the 18th of July, 1993. That is when I asked him to carry out an investigation about all these events and to inform his superiors. That is when the commander of Vitezovi launched an attack against Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. We can come back to that question. I'll look at my notes and we'll see if we want to come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. Please continue, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to continue along the lines that the Honourable Judges have touched upon. Tell me, General, according to the law, could you entrust anybody else with this investigation related to criminal acts except the SIS?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I could not entrust investigations of criminal acts to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Ante Sliskovic tell you most often? What were the sentences that he used when you asked him about the results of the investigation on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he would most often say, "The service is working, and when we complete the file, you will be informed about this." That was the report that I would receive most often all the way up to the end of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, if the local SIS in the Lasva River Valley would not get an order from the main SIS in Mostar, one that would be contrary to your orders, were Ante Sliskovic and the local SIS duty-bound to act on your instructions and orders and carry out an investigation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His office, was it in the Hotel Vitez or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He had an office in the Hotel Vitez, but he also had an office in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to have another document distributed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D580, D580A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is from the Defence Minister, representative of the Defence department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, and it was sent on the 1st of June, 1993. We're not going to read the contents of the document because that is not essential for my question, but we are just going to read who it was sent to, and could we have a focus on that on the ELMO, please, who it was delivered to directly by the Defence Ministry, and I'm reading that: Deliver to: Operative Zone, Southeast Herzegovina; Operative Zone, North-western Herzegovina; the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia; the Operative Zone of Bosanska Posavina; Professional Battalion, Vitezovi, Vitez; Professional Battalion, Petar Kresimir IV, Livno; Convicts Battalion; Bruno Busic unit; Personnel Administration of the Defence Department; Formations Section of the HVO main staff; the 106th Brcko Brigade; and the 115th Tuzla Brigade. I am now going to ask you, General: How do you explain the fact that on the 1st of June, 1993, the Defence Minister, to all intents and purposes, sends the same order to you, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, separately and separately to the Vitezovi? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that is an indicator at the same time. It shows that the chain of command, direct command, was retained by the defence department, going down towards the Professional Battalion of the Vitezovi on the 1st of June, 1993, and the entire period afterwards until the Professional Battalion was dismantled. So this is direct command and a direct chain of command down towards the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you recall this particular document? Do you remember having received it? Do you recognise the stamp and signature?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the contents of the document, and I also recognise the stamp and signature by the representative of the defence department, Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, independently of all that, we come to another question. In the course of 1992 and 1993, right up until the end of January 1994, in the Lasva Valley, was there ever -- did a unit of the Croatian army ever spend any time there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, never. It was never then or was it in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, units of the Croatian army, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now I would like to say a few words about trench-digging, ask you about that. Tell the Court, please, in the army, what is the general principle: When are fortifications dug, generally, trenches, communication trenches and so on, foxholes and so on?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there was a principle that was common knowledge from the first day you attended military academy, and that is to say, when you weren't using your rifle, you were using your picks and shovels; that is to say, when there was no fighting and when everything was calm on the battlefront, then you would engage in fortification, the digging of trenches, communicating trenches, foxholes and so on, and other work of that kind that will improve the defence qualities of the soldiers in their positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what is included in the front line of defence and what is the depth of a front line, according to military standards?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We have the fore section, the front section, that is to say, the soldiers' foxholes; then you have the trenches and communicating trenches along which the soldiers can move; then you have shelters where the soldiers are able to rest and sort of live; and then there are reserve positions which are at the rear end; and then you have access roads to all this which are used for the various shifts or to evacuate the wounded or for that kind of thing. Usually the depth of one battalion defending itself is between three to six kilometres. That is the general size. For a brigade, depending upon its intentions, it can be from 12 to 30 kilometres, that depth of the overall defence deployment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of this depth of the front line, in the Lasva Valley, for example, was there a rear in the true sense of the word from April 1993 to the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, and that was one of our greatest problems, in fact, because the maximum depth, because of the situation where we found ourselves, in total encirclement, was up to six kilometres, and it was one to one and a half kilometres at a minimum. So according to some military standards, army standards, we were not able to effect the full depth and deployment of the battalion as it took up its positions for defence which made the question of security more complex because there was no safe area where the soldiers could take shelter and rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We spoke about different military terms, foxholes, communicating trenches, shelters and the like, dugouts, access roads, and reserve positions, and we had problems with the translation of those terms. So on this piece of paper which we have put up on the easel, and I think we have something to write with, could you show us what each of these terms looks like? First of all, let's start with the foxholes, then the communicating trenches, the shelters, and the access roads.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps there is a darker felt-tip pen which would make the drawing more visible? Could you explain the symbols to us? What do the letters mean? What do each of these letters and shapes mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This position is what we call a Zarklon, foxhole, a position where a soldier is located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is the "Z" for "Zaklon"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Foxhole" in translation, interpreter adds.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And he has a defence assignment. If he has time, then he goes on to digging a communicating trench which should be a minimum of 100 to 150 metres away from the foxhole. And then we come to the shelter itself, Skloniste.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sk., interpreter adds.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which is in the background and, due to the configuration of the terrain, is also a sort of defended area, and eight to ten soldiers can sleep there. If anybody is wounded, then they are placed there and first aid can be administered. And then from the shelter, we would go on to reserve foxholes, communicating trenches, and, if possible, reserve shelters, and then the access roads to those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, the work platoons, the civilians making up the work platoons, where could those people do some work, work on which fortifications?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The work platoons are used to dig shelters and access roads leading up to those shelters, so they are not used to dig the foxholes and this part of the communicating trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose duty is it to dig out the foxholes and the communicating trenches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is the duty of each individual soldier, for himself, and once he takes up his defence position, because everybody wishes to adapt their position in such a way as to provide protection for them, and later on, when conditions are ripe, then the foxhole is dug out for a standing soldier. According to the JNA, it took a soldier 60 minutes to dig a foxhole of this kind using normal tools, and if he is to lie down, then this would take him 25 minutes, so these are the norms and standards of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We should like to tender this diagram into evidence, and it can be photocopied later on so that anybody interested can have a copy for themselves. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Defence Exhibit 581.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Document 301 and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't get the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- for the engineering assignments to be given, who did you order these assignments and who did you expect to do the digging, according to those orders of the 16th, 17th, and 18th of April when the hostile activities were taking place?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In those orders, once again, and in the orders directly issued via telephone, I issued direct orders to the commanders of the brigades that they should order their soldiers to start fortification work and to dig the foxholes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the record, the reference there was to D301 and D298.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that was what I heard from the French booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have the documents, we're not going to put them up on the ELMO, we've seen them many times, but I'm going to ask you a hypothetical question. Had you ordered, by issuing an order, to use the detained civilians, Muslims, to dig those trenches, I say hypothetically, once again, it is a question of principle, hypothetical, who would you have had to send the order to, had you made a decision which would be counter to the law of that kind?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I say, I never made a decision of that kind, but had I done so, I would have had to issue orders to the commander of a brigade, then to the commander of the military police, I would send him a request, a demand or order, and the head of the military district prison, the warden of the military district prison in charge of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would you send those orders to for trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The orders that I sent, I sent to the commanders of the brigades requesting, in very precise terms, that they issue orders to their own soldiers to undertake the fortification work and building of foxholes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in relation to the civilians taken prisoner, could they dig trenches or was that a violation of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was always my view that it was a violation of the Geneva Conventions. I always reacted to any violations, and this can be seen from Defence Exhibits D334.2, D362.2, D364.2 and D364.3, D365.1, D370.9, D376.1, D373 and D387. From those Defence Exhibits, my position was always very clear with regard to my stand on the use of prisoners, civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now have a few questions about the attack on Stari Vitez in 1993. Tell me, General, from April onwards up until the end of 1993, was Stari Vitez, for the citizens of Vitez, a problem? If so, why?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was a problem, mostly a security problem, because there were many civilian casualties, including children. They were hit by snipers and mortar fire from Stari Vitez towards the town of Vitez proper and the civilians of Vitez itself. This was an ongoing problem, a continuous problem, and there was always the demand made by the public, public opinion, that the problem of Stari Vitez be solved in a military fashion, that is to say, that a military drive be undertaken to neutralise the sources of that insecurity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite obviously, the military operation was not implemented, at least until the 18th of July, 1993. What was the view of the local politicians and public opinion with regard to that problem and in relation to yourself?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was always the culprit on duty, so to speak, and I was condemned and criticised for failing to take military action, that is, I suffered from public condemnation very frequently, especially when I spoke out at meetings of the Vitez government in May 1993 and when I said that there can be no military solution there and that I do not accept a military operation on Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because it was a built-up area, first and foremost, and it was a situation where the consequences of trying to solve the problem militarily would have been very bad with respect to the civilians living in Stari Vitez, because it would have been very difficult to avoid large scale destruction in Stari Vitez on the basis of a military operation in built-up areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you think? Darko Kraljevic, and you ascertained and so did SIS, that he launched this operation, why do you think he did launch it and carry it out?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was a local Vitez member, and I believe that he had several motives himself. One of those motives was to prove himself, to prove that he and his unit were able to undertake an operation of that kind which I did not dare implement myself. I also believe that that operation, had it succeeded, would have increased his popularity and his powers of command and would have, in a way, enabled him to have even more power and authority in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the present situation, looking back with the hindsight that you have with the passage of time and the knowledge that you have gained throughout this trial and so forth, what is your opinion? Why was the attack launched when you went to -- the operation, why did it take place when you went to Busovaca for the weekend?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I now believe that that attack was not launched by chance when I happened to be absent, because by the very fact that I was absent I was not able to wield any influence on the situation, nor could I prevent the attack from taking place. It was common knowledge, my position was common knowledge with regard to the Stari Vitez problem because I never allowed an operation to be launched on Stari Vitez itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On several occasions during this trial, you saw document D250, and that is the report of the Vitezovi about their work in '92/'93, so let's not look at the document, if possible. Can you remember what it says in this report? Who ordered the attack on Stari Vitez in the report written by the Vitezovi themselves?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In document 250, it says that the action was ordered by the commander of the Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic, and he told me that himself when I came back to Vitez. When I asked him who carried out this action and on whose orders, he said that it was on his orders that this action was carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the artillery used in this action, the artillery that was otherwise under your command? I'm referring to heavy artillery.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was not used, and I'm sure that it was not even requested, that is to say, to use this artillery that was under my command, because in that case, the commander of the artillery certainly would have asked me for my approval. In this way, he would have informed me about this action, and I believe that it was intentional, that this request was not sent to have the artillery used in order to conceal the preparation for this action and the action itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, you mentioned some kind of an imitation multiple rocket launcher. Could you tell me in a few sentences what all this was about, this imitator of the multiple rocket launcher, of the VBR?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that it was the craftsmen of Vitez who made this imitator of the VBR, the multiple rocket launcher. It made the same kind of noise that a multiple rocket launcher does, and it was used to boost the morale of the local troops of the HVO and to demoralise the enemy, that is to say, the members of the BH army. I know that it was an electric device, and it concentrated on making the same kind of noise that a multiple rocket launcher does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, in fact, could it have launched anything explosive?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, it just made the kind of noise that a multiple rocket launcher does, but it cannot launch anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came back from Busovaca, what did you hear in relation to this action aimed at Stari Vitez, briefly?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was informed that the fighting was not intensive, that the operation was carried out poorly, from a military point of view, and that there were 14 to 15 soldiers on the HVO side that were killed and that the BH army had celebrated a victory in that action. Also, there were a large number of soldiers from the HVO that were wounded as a consequence of the reaction and the artillery fire of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Stari Vitez and from other positions, all of this directed against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time, the International Community, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or your subordinates, did anybody put a question or did anybody inform you about the use of the so-called "babies," that is, in this action against Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. After that, I had many meetings with representatives of UNPROFOR, of the UNHCR, the International Red Cross. Later, there were meetings with the representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. No one ever put any questions related to the use of "babies," and I first heard about this here in this courtroom from certain witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to have a document distributed now, please. We are going to talk about Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Defence Exhibit D582, 582A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please take a quick look at this document. We're not going to read all of it. I just want you to remember what this document is all about, and then I'm going to put a question to you. This document is dated the 10th of September, 1993, and could you please tell us, what is the authority that composed this document, and do you recognise the seal and the signature?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is a document of the civilian police station from Vitez. I recognise the signature. That is the signature of the commander of the police station, Kresimir Garic. The stamp is of the civilian police of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read the first sentence, and then let us see which is the village concerned. I'm starting: "Report on the investigation that has been carried out on the terrain and objects in the immediate vicinity of the British units of UNPROFOR located in Stara Bila, Vitez municipality." Please tell the Court the following: Which is this terrain and what are these objects? What is this that the civilian police inspected? Which village are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: D582 pertains to the village of Grbavica, that area of the village that the civilian police arrived at on the 8th of September, '93. They took over the security in this area, and then after they took over this area and carried out this blockade, then they started doing their police work, that is to say, searching the entire area of Grbavica and all the objects, that is to say, all the buildings, facilities, that are in the wider area of Grbavica on the 8th and on the next day also, the 9th of September, 1993, together with UNPROFOR forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, remind us: When was the military operation that you commanded completed? Which day, which hour?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The military action ended on the 8th of September, 1993, around 1430, that is to say, in the afternoon, and after that, the civilian police arrived, they sealed off the entire area, they took over the security, and they started doing routine work, that is to say, searching the entire area and all the buildings and facilities in the territory of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why it was decided that the civilian police should take over the village of Grbavica after the army managed to repel the BH army and to drive them out of that stronghold?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The army had to remain in close contact with the BH army because it was only to be expected that the BH army would carry out a counterattack, and it was the regular duty of the civilian police force to have total control over a territory and it is their professional task to secure the area, to search the area, and to work in built-up areas. So this is their professional and functional duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are not going to read the document; it is self-explanatory. Now I would like to move on to another subject, and those are "babies." Tell me, General, how were "babies" created? Was this on orders? How was this explosive device made in the first place?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is a product that was made by the workers from the military factory. It was not on orders. This was an improvised device which was never in the organisational or formational composition of any HVO unit, that is to say, it never became part of standard equipment, but it did exist, and from time to time it was used by soldiers at the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that "babies" were being used? If you did, under what circumstances were these "babies" used, as a rule?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had received information to the effect that "babies" were being used, most often at the front line under circumstances when we would run out of ammunition and when these improvised devices were used in our attempts to try to repel enemy attacks, and we tried to get these "babies" into the shelters or trenches of the enemy ranks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that "babies" were used at the front line, what are you trying to say? Are you talking about front lines in built-up areas, or what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, as far as built-up areas are concerned, my position was very well-known and my orders were well-known too, that artillery should not be used against built-up areas, and that was the case of Stari Vitez as well. The command of the Operative Zone never issued orders to have artillery used against Stari Vitez. So "babies" were not used in built-up areas, in populated areas; they were used only in certain hills, certain positions, and certain key points that were held by the HVO outside these villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another subject that was mentioned in cross-examination, that is, the village of Gacice and a few things related to the village of Gacice. Did you receive information that the civilians of the village of Gacice came to the centre of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not receive such information that civilians had come. I already mentioned that at that time, on the 20th of April, I was at a meeting in Zenica, and I did not receive such information until I went to the meeting in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you heard about the ... Perhaps the interpretation was not accurate. Could you please tell me when you found out that there were civilians? Did you hear about this in the courtroom, when you were in Zenica, or before or after Zenica? When did you hear about the civilians from Gacice in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That information, that civilians had been brought into town, the town of Vitez, I found this out from an operative report of the Vitez Brigade, that civilians were brought in front of the -- but that they were brought in front of a hotel, that they were in front of the hotel. I first heard about this from a protected witness here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're not going to mention who this witness was, we are not going to mention any names, but on the basis of what you heard here in the courtroom, what is your conclusion? Was this, in fact, a human shield or not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that this was not a human shield because when these civilians were brought in, Vitez was not exposed to artillery fire; during the stay of these civilians also, it was not exposed to artillery fire; and also during the time of the return of these civilians to their village, Vitez was not exposed to artillery fire. It is my opinion that this was an irresponsible local commander who had, at his own initiative, brought these civilians and who later on received the right order, that is to say, to return these civilians to their village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These civilians lived in their village after the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina left Gacice. However, you were accused by international factors precisely because of these civilians and precisely because they were living in their village. What was all of this about? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were two approaches there that often put me in a position where I did not know how to act; that is to say, that officials of the International Red Cross, Mr. de la Mota and Ms. Margaret Green, said that civilians in that village felt like hostages and that they were being kept against their own free will in their own village and that they all wanted to go to stay with their husbands who were in an area that was under control of the BH army. At that time, I told the officials of the International Red Cross that these civilians were not hostages but that it was our duty, in respect of the UNHCR position, to protect these civilians and that I had issued such orders to brigade commanders. It is probably such orders that were being carried out, because if these civilians were ever to leave, the UNHCR would have characterised this as ethnic cleansing. The International Red Cross officials asked for all civilians to be given absolute freedom of movement in a civil war; and in the situation that we were in, I told them, the Red Cross officials, that that would only mean freedom of departure, freedom to leave their homes and to go to territory that was under the control of their own army. In this case, it was the Muslims who wanted to go to BH army-controlled territory, just as Croats came and wanted to come to HVO-controlled territories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, General, did you ultimately organise their transport out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I worked in that situation and, first of all, I received information from UNHCR officials. I had asked them to clarify their mandate to me, and they said that they were in charge of these matters and that their position was, vis-à-vis civilians in such situations, that they be given all protection and that no resettlement be carried out. I also remember very well that with regard to this problem of Gacice, the local commander, his name was Matic, stood in front of the U.N. vehicle and explained to the U.N. patrol that he had orders to give protection to civilians and to prevent any kind of resettlement in anybody's organisation. I found out later that the civilians had left but not with the participation of the army of the HVO and the HVO military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to have another document distributed, please. This new document actually has two original texts; namely, in 1993, the author of this document authored two versions, the English and the Croatian language versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D583 and D583A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to read the heading and several points from the document. We're not going to read the whole of it. It says: The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Forward Command Department for the Vitez municipality. The number is official and the date is the 20th of May, 1993, and it is a report on activities related to the civil affairs office with regard to releasing persons detained. It is sent to the European Monitoring Mission, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, UNPROFOR, the UNHCR, the International Red Cross, the HVO government - Vitez, and Dario Kordic of the HZ-HB, and the text was compiled by the coordinator of the department, Pero Skopljak, MA. General, do you remember the contents of the document and the signature of Mr. Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Pero Skopljak's signature I do recognise, yes, and the contents of the document speaks of activities, we called it the Department for Exchange and Liberation of Detained Persons, and that was on behalf of the civilian authorities led by Mr. Pero Skopljak and on behalf of the authorities of the Bosniak Muslims, Mrs. Emira Bolic headed that section, and they cooperated directly on matters of exchange and the release of detained persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, from the heading, we can see the social activities department of Vitez. Was that department within the composition of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone or within the civilian organs of power and authority?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was within the power of the civilian organs of authority because there was another department attached to the government of the HVO, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, with its headquarters in Mostar, and it is functioning today. I think today it deals more with questions of finding detained persons and locating corpses as well, but that department is functioning today and works with the same sort of questions, but this is a department for the Vitez area and it is within the composition of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the document and from what you have said, who, after the 16th of April, 1993, was in charge of detained persons, particularly civilian detainees, in the Vitez area: the Central Bosnia Operative Zone or the civilian organs of power and authority?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the civilian organs of power and authority that were in charge on the basis of an agreement signed previously and they were in charge of those sorts of activities, and they would inform us from time to time, through reports of this kind, about what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military conscripts, civilians, Muslims, males, they found themselves arrested, detained, and were sent to the cinema in Vitez, somewhere in the chess club in the SDK building and so on. Did you order those arrests?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not. I never ordered those arrests, I never permitted them, nor did I know that such arrests would take place. When I learnt of them, I ordered that humane treatment be implemented and that these individuals be treated as humanely as possible, and, of course, I did everything to ensure an exchange and release for those individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not unilaterally let them out into the streets from the cinema? You said you heard about this fairly soon after they were arrested. Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that it was not up to me, my discretionary right, to release individuals, and the practice was such, that is to say, I learnt this practice from the International Red Cross, and I was duty-bound to adhere to the protocol of the International Red Cross about the release of detained persons or arrested persons. Second, the situation itself was highly unstable, particularly at the time when there still had not been a cease-fire in effect. It was a highly precarious situation. There were private arrests being made too and private exchanges taking place by different groups and extremist groups as well, and I thought that, in a situation of this kind when fighting was still going on, it would be highly unsafe to release the prisoners, and I would also have violated the protocol of the International Red Cross by so doing. In document 318, I issued an order that the civilians be released but the situation had to become stable, first of all, and to ensure that the International Red Cross take all the steps according to their mandate which came before the actual release of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of these civilians ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, should I understand your position to have been this, that once individuals were in your custody, you were powerless to release them without the approval of the International Red Cross? Was that your understanding of the position?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I understood it, and had anybody -- whenever anybody was registered, he would have had to have been -- his name taken down by the International Red Cross and, according to its protocol, be released. That was the number one condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So that if you yourself wanted to release individuals today but it took two or three weeks to acquire the approval of the International Red Cross, you would have to await the giving of that approval before you could release them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is how I understood it. I would have had to have waited, although the Red Cross had access, and we never would have waited two weeks. The basic problem was for the fighting to stop and for the situation to be safe and secure, but it was the supreme position of the International Red Cross that there should be a registration, first of all, that all the detained persons should have been questioned, and then after that had been done, released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are you saying that the position was this: The actual release of anyone who was in your custody depended on approval by the Red Cross of the security climate into which those persons were to be released?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Primarily, it was the protocol of the Red Cross and their mandate which was duty-binding for us -- which was binding for us, that is to say, we would have to enable them to do their part of the job first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. We have been working for an hour and twenty minutes. I suppose, Mr. Nobilo, that you, who always checked the time spent by the parties very carefully, but you know that the Judges consider this question of time very flexibly, do you still need a long time to ask your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No. Four to five questions, and that's all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I think we will still take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Nobilo, we can resume now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few more questions about the car bomb. Had you known that a truck bomb, that is to say, a truck with an explosive, was being made ready, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have, of course, prevented has terrorist act and would have undertaken everything in my power to prevent such an action from taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Vitezovi able to expect this kind of stand on your part?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was general knowledge that I had previously issued orders demanding that all perpetrators be brought to justice from the HVO and that I always strove to have the law respected. In that sense, I issued a series of documents. I think that it was common knowledge that I would have reacted in order prevent activities of that kind had I known of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, did the Vitezovi have a reason to hide an action of this kind from you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the preparation and the implementation of that action because they could have expected my reactions to it, and I was absolutely certain that they had every reason to hide the preparations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor mentioned several witnesses from Dr. Mujezinovic onwards who had certain knowledge as to what was being prepared on the eve of the explosion, the truck explosion in Stari Vitez. How do you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think that is correct because Dr. Mujezinovic, in his testimony, said that he received this information from Mr. Katava, that an explosion had taken place in an ammunitions warehouse, and that was the information I received from the commander of the Vitez Brigade immediately after the explosion. Next, another witness, Sefik Pezer, said that shelling was expected, so that was not correct either in relation to what actually happened. Then once again, Witness A and Witness E, that something was being prepared and that they had allegedly received information from a woman Croat whose husband was in the HVO, perhaps her husband was in the Vitezovi, a member of the Vitezovi, and so perhaps he had some information as to preparations going on. Also, Defence witness Marijan Strukar, who was at the scene of the crime, learned several minutes before the explosion took place. Probably he was warned for security reasons to move away from the area, but he didn't have any information about the preparation of such a terrorist act either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, what were you doing in general terms? What were your activities on that day?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That can be seen from the chronology of my testimony, that is to say, that I was engaged in commanding combat operations because the fighting was intense, and from one minute to the next, I communicated with my commanders. I was not in a position to leave my duties in that regard and to walk around town and collect information as to what was going on where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On several occasions in the course of this trial, in great detail, you spoke about your competencies and authorisations, and also on many occasions in the course of the trial, you said that you did not have the power to command the military police and the civilian police force when they were undertaking criminal investigations and to tell them what to do. However, nonetheless, there are documents in the file which were sent to the military police, for example, and which were titled as orders, and they refer to investigations and disciplinary measures to be taken against certain policemen. How do you explain that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to the law on criminal proceedings, my role was a peripheral one as commander, and I truly did not have the power and authority to uncover the perpetrators of criminal acts. But I did exert pressure and insisted that the services, the military police, the security services, should do everything in their power to identify the perpetrators. Very often, in these requests of mine, I used formal documents linked to orders, but I did not have any competency to issue orders with regard to detection and criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you use the term "order"? Why didn't you use another term which would be more in line with criminal proceedings, like a criminal report or file criminal charges or something of that kind? Why did you use the term "order," the word "order"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were situations in which I endeavoured to exert pressure on these services and to demand that they improve the quality of their work, to uncover crime, and it is evident that if I formulate this demand as an order, then the relationship towards what I was asking for would be different. But for an order to be an order in the military sense of the word, the possibility for sanctioning would have to stand behind it if the order were not carried out, and in my case, I had no competencies of that kind, nor could I undertake any sanctions, disciplinary measures, if orders of this kind were not carried out, so that orders of this kind were reduced to voluntary relationship towards -- an arbitrary relationship towards these documents that I issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your military training, were you trained to deal with laterally positioned organs who were placed at your disposal and were not under your command? What acts were you taught and what about this hierarchy? How did it function with regard to what you were taught in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army, there was unity of command, and it was subordinated and defined in such a way that the commander in a given area was directly superior to all those institutions. There was no parallelism in command, in the chain of command, and there was no duality of command within the JNA, and we did not encounter such cases in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A commander in the JNA, how would he ask the military police to conduct an investigation? What were you trained?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the JNA, exclusively in the form of an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We're now going to hand round the last document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we do so and while we're waiting for the document to be handed round, I want to ask you a question that was asked to you by the President of the Trial Chamber, that is to say, whether the policy in the HVO was that crimes were not reported.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that was not the policy, and from the very time that I came to head it, I always wanted to enforce law and order and issued an order which held true for all time, that all perpetrators of crimes should be disarmed and removed from the units and that the competent departments of defence should give them another assignment, which was usually a work assignment, not a military assignment. As I say, that was not the practice, and I always strove for legality within the HVO to be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May we give a number to this last document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 584, 584A for the English version, and this is a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the decree on internal affairs during the state of war or in danger of war on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This is the Official Gazette number 2, this is a public document, that is to say, and it regulates the way in which the civilian police operates. I'm just asking you the following: Did you command the civilian police or was this some autonomous organisation in relation to your authority?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not command the civilian police, and it is obvious from this decree that the civilian police was organised through its own departments, the police administrations, and it was beyond my authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On several occasions, the Prosecutor showed Narodne Novine, the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia, and it was obvious that many people from Central Bosnia were decorated by the president of the state of Croatia, like Slavko Marin, Edvard Tolo, Mladen Holman, et cetera, not to enumerate all of them. Tell the Court whether you were ever decorated by Croatia or did you ever receive any kind of decoration?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never received any decoration from the Republic of Croatia or Herceg-Bosna. I got a decoration on the 23rd of October, 1992, that is to say, the Golden Lily, in the building of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo. It was conferred upon me there, together with two other officers from the HVO, and that session was chaired by Mr. Ejub Ganic, and I think that General Morillon was at that meeting in the building of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is a military decoration that was conferred upon members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At first, when you came to The Hague, you heard the indictment and also you saw the amended indictment, and now we are nearing the end of this trial. Could you please tell the Court what your attitude is now in respect of the indictment? Do you feel guilty or not with regard to the charges brought against you in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not feel guilty with regard to any one of the counts in the indictment, and I think that during my testimony, I tried to present everything before this Honourable Court, and I'm sure that I honourably, conscientiously carried out my duties in a situation of a civil war while there was a total military encirclement, while facing a totally superior enemy, and I tried to ensure our survival in the enclave and in the Lasva pocket. I had to deal with tens of thousands of refugees that I had to receive, and I'm convinced that I did everything that was within my command authority and everything that I knew how to do, on the basis of my military knowledge, in order to prevent any violence committed against civilians, to prevent the repetition of any crimes, and to ensure changes in the organisational structure of the HVO, which would make it possible for me to considerably improve upon public law and order and general security in the area that I commanded later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence rests. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for having respected the time limit that you had been set, and we know that the witness was able to express himself over these long weeks of cross-examination and direct examination. The Judges themselves asked many questions. There may still be a few questions left. Let me turn to Judge Shahabuddeen. Do you have any further questions you would like to ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just a few. These relate to the early period of the testimony of the witness. You will recall that during that period, it was still the practice of members of the bench not to intervene in the course of examination with questions. We later changed that practice. But there are only a few questions, General. You remember that you were talking about your training period, and you told us that the practice then was that all ethnic groups would mix together in the training system. Would that have included people from all parts of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, in principle, all were included, from all parts. However, those persons who were born in the territory where the garrison in question was were not included. For example, people from Postinje could not do their military service in Postinje and get their military training there. However, there were persons from all other republics there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You told us of a practice of sending army units to act as police forces in Kosovo for the purpose of intimidating the population there, and that in opposition to this policy, you refused to go to Kosovo, although there was an extra wartime allowance for going to that area. If I am recalling your evidence correctly, was that practice, of using the army for missions of intimidation into Kosovo, in existence at the same time when there was this training practice of including all ethnic groups within the training system?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this practice existed precisely at the time when the members of all ethnic groups took part. However, the selection of manpower, of personnel that would be chosen, was particularly carried out at that time by the military security forces and a particular selection was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And it was because you didn't like this policy that you elected to pursue civilian studies in the field of business and law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was not a supporter of that kind of policy and such engagement of the military, although, in addition to the wartime allowance, there were other bonuses, that is to say, in terms of promotions. Everybody who would take this upon himself would get many privileges. These extra wartime allowances were only one of them, and I did not take any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The SFRY, the old Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was still in existence at that time, was it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This was 1985 and 1986. It still existed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to Ahmici. You said it was portrayed in the media as a victory or as a great victory gained by the HVO over the Armija but that you never thought it was a victory.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time I said that that was the public opinion that prevailed, that is to say, sometime in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, meetings were held on a daily basis at which you presided. Was that media projection of Ahmici as "a great victory" discussed by anyone at any of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the sense of being a victory, it was not discussed that way at the meetings that I chaired over my own team because this was a very short but intensive period. It was overwhelming in terms of the number of events that were taking place, and we concentrated on trying to have a cease-fire in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is my impression correct, that of all of these many incidents which were taking place at the same time, the operation at Ahmici was being presented in the media as the greatest of all HVO victories at the time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour, that at that time the TV was broadcasting, that this videotape that was presented here in court was ever shown on local television. But on the basis of the report that I heard here on that videotape, I heard the speaker saying that this was a military victory. He had made this video footage, apparently, and he said it was a victory, but I personally had never seen this tape before I came here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: My recollection is that you also said that you personally never considered it a victory.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. From a military point of view and on the basis of the information I have today, it is no victory at all, and I did not consider it to be a victory at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So there was a contradiction between your personal assessment of the military significance of Ahmici and the public presentation of the event. Was there a contradiction, do you think?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I look at the military significance of the village as such, it does not have any military significance. The positions above the village have certain military significance, but the village as such, I don't see any military significance there. However, the media were operated by local cameramen who did not have any military knowledge, I think, so then they worked according to certain suggestions or certain instructions and they presented such things to the public in keeping with what they thought. I never told them "Tape this" or "Tape that" or "Launch such and such a piece of information." I presented my opinion concerning Ahmici at the press conference. I condemned this, I qualified it as a crime, and everything else I pointed out at the press conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So your assessment of the event was at variance with the public presentation of it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, when I received more complete information on everything that had happened, it was at variance, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. I thought it was at variance. What I wanted to ask you, General, was this: Since there was such a variance, did you feel obliged to point out the variance at any of these daily meetings which were being held?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already testified that I indeed did not have all the information that I had the opportunity of hearing over here, but my first reaction was, when I heard the indictment in relation to this at the meeting in Zenica, I reacted to it. I talked to my associates about it. Also, when I got that letter from Colonel Stewart, again I convened a meeting of my immediate team, and I publicly said what I had to say. On the 27th of April, I said in public that Ahmici was a crime and that an investigation would follow and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I apologise, General, if I led you into the area of the criminality of whatever was done. What I had in mind was this: When you opined that Ahmici was not a military victory, I gathered that you were basing that assessment on the military significance of the village and not on the facts relating to the event which took place there of which you learned later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ahmici does not have any military significance in any case, that is to say, the position of the village does not have any military significance. I had received information about the combat operations taking place between the BH army and the HVO, and it is the facilities above Ahmici that have military significance, and I had received information that the HVO was there but, actually, it never was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You had received information that the HVO was above Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the end of the first day, I think, sometime in the evening, that the HVO had passed through the village and that it was moving on to positions above Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That was on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, approximately on the 16th of April in the early evening or evening hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us talk about the evening of the 15th of April going over to the 16th of April. At that point of time, as commanding officer of the HVO, what was your expectation of the likely movement of the Armija? Was it the case that, in your judgement, the Armija was expected to come down the Kuber mountains or the Kuber hills, whatever they were, I'm not sure?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're right, Kuber is a mountain, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It's a mountain.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're right. It's much bigger than a hill. I did not expect them to go down immediately because, first of all, this position had to be taken over and it's quite massive, so I did expect fighting to take place at Kuber, and I thought that the Armija would try to take over this position in the fullest sense of the word. Then, as far as further operative developments are concerned, then it was -- it was a different situation. It could have been used vis-à-vis Busovaca and vis-à-vis Vitez. So the first thing that had to be done, at any rate, was to take Kuber and to create an operative basis for further activity in possible directions, those that were made available to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So, General, if I have grasped the topography correctly, at that point of time, the Armija was some distance east of Ahmici; they had not yet come down the Kuber Mountain.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time was in Ahmici too. This is a battalion of the 325th Brigade whose command post was at Poculica or Preocica. I think Poculica, rather. In Ahmici, I think there was a company there, the 3rd Company of the 2nd Battalion, I think, of the 325th Brigade from Vitez, of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the other forces of the 3rd Corps were at Kuber, that is to say, some other brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now I understand you. So the Armija had elements in Ahmici, but the bulk of the forces of the Armija were expected to come down the Kuber Mountain; is that about correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A part of the forces, the main forces, certainly, they went down. They were coming from Zenica. However, the main forces of the 325th Vitez Brigade was in Kruscica. That is where the commander was and the command post and the main forces of the 325th Brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, could the HVO go into Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, could the HVO, on that date, go into Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understood your question properly, Your Honour. Are you referring to whether it was possible to pass by Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That's a better way, I admit, of putting the intent of my questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, tensions were heightened, that is what the situation was, but there weren't any barricades yet. The situation was rather tense. I think that it was possible to pass there but with extra caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So I understand the position on the 15th to have been this, that the situation in Ahmici was tense but that subject to that, the HVO could pass through the village.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether they could pass through the village actually, that is to say, the situation was tense throughout the Vitez area. There were meetings, lower level meetings held between the representatives of the BH army and the HVO, there were meetings between civilian representatives of power and authority, and we did expect that this tension would be overcome and that there would be no conflict. So I'm not quite sure -- well, yes, the situation was similar in Kruscica and the whole Vitez municipality. Tensions were present in Travnik as well, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
